newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania opposition angry over OSCE team withdrawal.
newsitem.headline: Albania opposition angry over OSCE team withdrawal.

text.p: Albania's opposition Socialists on Thursday slammed the government for barring a team of election monitors from observing Albania's municipal polls on Sunday, calling the step an "act of primitive revenge".

Observers from a branch of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said on Wednesday they would not monitor the polls after the government of President Sali Berisha approved only part of its proposed list of observers.

"This is an expression of primitive revenge against the unbiased and objective stand of this organisation which compiled a detailed report on the massive violations during the May 26 elections," the Socialist Party said in a statement.
It added the move hinted at new isolationist tendencies in the small Balkan nation where communism was toppled in 1990.
Berisha's ruling Democratic Party is still smarting from criticism by the OSCE branch, the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR), of Albania's general elections in May and June.
Most opposition parties withdrew from that poll, alleging the ballot was rigged, and refused to take up the seats they won. The Democrats secured 89 percent of the vote.
Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Tritan Shehu criticised the team's decision, telling a news conference: "This creates a crisis of trust between us and the ODIHR mission, but not the OSCE."

Criticising the ODIHR for their report on the controversial May 26 election, Shehu said the government was suprised the OSCE mission had submitted a list with 37 observers for the municipal polls instead of the originally agreed 15.
ODIHR cancelled its mission after the list was rejected, saying the number of observers it sent to monitor elections was not a matter for negotiations with host governments.

The United States and the 15-nation European Union have sent clear signals to Berisha's conservative government that they will be watching closely this weekend for signs of Albania's commitment to democracy.

The municipal poll will be monitored by up to 500 international observers coordinated by the Council of Europe, the forum set up to promote human rights across the continent. The OSCE itself is expected to send 12 observers.
Some 2.2 million Albanians are eligible to vote in the elections for councils at town, district and communal level.
